Dropping two trailing segments can collapse two distinct fault-injector configs onto the same derived DB name, and since the suites use that name for `delete_prev_db`/`create_db`, two parametrizations will create and delete the same database and interfere with each other. Either scope the new split to the newly added (standalone) configs or verify it against every existing config name returned by the injector.

`set_maint_notifications_pool_handler_for_connection()` / `set_maint_notifications_cluster_handler_for_connection()` wire the parser handlers and the connection-level handler onto an *existing* connection, but never initialize `orig_host_address` / `orig_socket_timeout` / `orig_socket_connect_timeout` (those are only set inside `_configure_maintenance_notifications`, which is skipped when the connection was built with maintenance notifications disabled). `_update_maint_notifications_configs_for_connections()` uses exactly this path when `update_maint_notifications_config()` turns the feature on for a pool that was created with it off, so the first `reset_tmp_settings()` on such a connection — from `handle_maintenance_completed_notification`, from MOVING cleanup, or from the new `disconnect()` hook that calls `reset_tmp_settings(reset_relaxed_timeout=True)` when the state is MAINTENANCE — raises AttributeError inside the push-notification path. Set the orig_* snapshot when the handler is attached (the sync file has the same gap, so fix both).

kwargs assembly ordering: the `unix_socket_path` branch forces `"maint_notifications_config": MaintNotificationsConfig(enabled=False)`, but the later unconditional `if maint_notifications_config: kwargs.update({"maint_notifications_config": maint_notifications_config})` overwrites it with the user's config (any config instance is truthy), so the forced disable is dead code. Worse, the RESP3 guard right above it is not skipped for unix sockets: `Redis(unix_socket_path=..., protocol=2, maint_notifications_config=MaintNotificationsConfig())` (enabled="auto") now raises RedisError even though the branch just decided the feature is unsupported/disabled for this connection type. Move the RESP3 validation and the config forwarding into the TCP branch (or skip both when `unix_socket_path` is set).

The new `maint_notifications_config` constructor argument is not documented in the `RedisCluster` class docstring, which enumerates every user-facing constructor parameter with `:param ...:`. Per CONTRIBUTING (docstrings must be updated for user-facing changes) and for parity with the async `Redis` client — which does document it — add a `:param maint_notifications_config:` entry.

`DEFAULT_SOCKET_TIMEOUT = 5` is hardcoded here and shadows the library constant of the same name, while the sync sibling (`tests/maint_notifications/test_cluster_maint_notifications_handling.py`) and `tests/maint_notifications/test_async_maint_notifications_handling.py` use `redis._defaults.DEFAULT_SOCKET_TIMEOUT`. Import the constant (or give the local one a distinct name such as `TEST_SOCKET_TIMEOUT`) so the sibling suites do not silently diverge if the default changes.

`ensure_connection()` now suppresses the "Connection has data" / "Connection not ready" guard whenever `maint_notifications_enabled()` is truthy. Because the pool auto-creates a default `MaintNotificationsConfig()` (enabled="auto") for every RESP3 pool, this effectively disables dirty-connection detection for all RESP3 async users, not just those who opted into maintenance notifications. A connection returned to the pool with unread response bytes (e.g. a cancelled read) will now be silently reused and desynchronise the request/response stream. Consider draining pending push frames instead of skipping the check entirely, or only skipping when a push frame is actually pending.

The new maintenance-state reset at the end of `AbstractConnection.disconnect()` is unreachable on two early-return paths in the same method: the `asyncio.current_task() is None` fast path at the top, and the `if not self.is_connected: return` inside the timeout block. A connection that is disconnected via either path while in `MaintenanceState.MAINTENANCE` keeps the relaxed `socket_timeout`/`socket_connect_timeout` and the MAINTENANCE state after reconnecting, so the relaxation is never rolled back unless a completion notification happens to arrive later.

The maintenance guard was added asymmetrically in the sync pools. `BlockingConnectionPool.get_connection()` gained `and self.cache is None and not self.maint_notifications_enabled()` on *both* `can_read()` checks, but `ConnectionPool.get_connection()` only got it on the post-reconnect check; the first `can_read()` check in that method is untouched by this diff. If that first check still lacks the maintenance guard, an idle connection holding a pending push frame will raise "Connection has data", be caught by the surrounding `except`, and be disconnected/reconnected on every acquire — dropping the maintenance notification and thrashing connections. Please verify both checks are guarded consistently.

`ProxyServerFaultInjector` loses `execute_failover`/`execute_migrate`/`execute_rebind` and raises `NotImplementedError` from `get_slot_migrate_triggers` / `get_topology_change_standalone_triggers`. The standalone scenario tests were simultaneously converted to `@pytest.mark.parametrize(..., generate_params(_FAULT_INJECTOR_STANDALONE_CLIENT, ...))`, and `generate_params` swallows the exception and returns `[]`. Under `use_mock_proxy()` every standalone maintenance-notification scenario test therefore collects zero cases and silently passes, whereas before this change those tests actually exercised the mock proxy. Either implement the trigger endpoints for the proxy injector or make `generate_params` fail loudly instead of returning an empty list.

The `fault_injector_client` fixture now returns `AsyncProxyServerFaultInjector` when `use_mock_proxy()` is set, but `tests/test_asyncio/test_scenario/test_active_active.py::trigger_network_failure_action` calls `fault_injector_client.trigger_action()` / `get_action_status()`, which only exist on `AsyncREFaultInjector` (they are not part of the `AsyncFaultInjectorClient` ABC). Running the async active-active suite with the mock proxy enabled will fail with `AttributeError` instead of skipping.

`HImportRegistry.get()` is annotated `-> HImportFieldset | None` and this new module has no `from __future__ import annotations` (its imports are only `threading`, `collections.abc`, `dataclasses`, `redis.exceptions`, `redis.typing`). PEP 604 unions between a class and `None` are evaluated at def time and raise `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |` on Python 3.9, which README still advertises as supported. Because `redis/client.py` now imports `redis._himport_exec` -> `redis.himport` at module scope, this makes plain `import redis` fail on 3.9. Use `Optional[HImportFieldset]` or add the `__future__` import.

The "cosmetic" `status_code: str = None` -> `str | None = None` change introduces PEP 604 syntax into `redis/exceptions.py`. Unless this module carries `from __future__ import annotations`, these parameter annotations are evaluated at import time and raise TypeError on Python 3.9 (still supported per README), breaking `import redis` entirely. The same concern applies to the two new PEP 604 annotations added in this PR to modules that otherwise still use `Optional[...]`: `himport_registry: HImportRegistry | None = None` in `redis/connection.py` (AbstractConnection.__init__) and in `redis/cluster.py` (NodesManager.__init__). Please verify each of those files has the `__future__` import, or keep `Optional[...]`.

`ConnectionPool.__init__` now injects `himport_registry` into `connection_kwargs` unconditionally (same in `redis/asyncio/connection.py`), so every connection is constructed as `connection_class(himport_registry=..., **rest)`. Any third-party/user-defined `connection_class` with an explicit `__init__` signature (a documented extension point) will now fail with `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'himport_registry'` on first connection — a silent breaking change for a runtime dependency. It also leaks an internal object into the public `Redis.get_connection_kwargs()` result. Consider the approach already used in `NodesManager.create_redis_node`: keep the registry on the pool and assign it onto the connection object after construction (in `make_connection`) instead of passing it as a constructor kwarg.

`himport_prepare`/`himport_discard`/`himport_discard_all` are defined on `Redis` and read `self._single_connection_client`, but `Pipeline.__init__` does not set that attribute (it does not call `Redis.__init__`), so the README-documented `pipe.himport_prepare("users", [...])` inside a `with r.pipeline() as pipe:` block will raise `AttributeError`. The async mirror is worse: `redis/asyncio/client.py::himport_prepare` starts with `await self.initialize()`, which reads `self.single_connection_client` — also unset on the async `Pipeline`. No test covers calling these methods on a standalone pipeline (the integration tests call them on the client). Either guard with `getattr(self, ...)`/override on `Pipeline`, or drop the pipeline usage from the README example, and add a test for it.

`himport_prepare_internal`, `himport_discard_internal` and `himport_discard_all_internal` are new public command methods for a feature that is not in a GA server (the CI map now points 8.10 at `8.10-rc2`, and the tests are gated on 8.9.0 while CURRENT_REDIS_VERSION is 8.8.0), yet they lack the `@experimental_method()` decorator that `himport_set` and the client-level `himport_*` methods carry. Their docstrings also omit the `Available since Redis X.Y` line used by other recently added commands. Per repo policy every command method targeting an unreleased Redis feature must be decorated.

The HIMPORT note added to `slave_for` is a copy of the `master_for` note and is misleading for a replica client: it says the fieldset survives failover because "the pool re-points to the new master" and ends with "(`himport_set` is a write and is served by the master)", but a client from `slave_for` will get a READONLY error for `himport_set`. Also, both new notes contain a garbled sentence — "Each call to current method returns" / "Each call to current command returns" in `redis/asyncio/sentinel.py`. Please fix the wording and drop/adjust the write-related sentence for `slave_for` in both the sync and async files.

`TestIsHImportSetCommand` carries `@pytest.mark.fixed_client` twice (duplicated decorator), while the immediately following `TestHImportAskRedirectSync` — which is the only HIMPORT test class without the marker — appears to be the intended target of the second one. Remove the duplicate and mark the sync ASK-redirect class if it needs the marker.

`himport_prepare` / `himport_discard` / `himport_discard_all` are defined on `Redis` and dereference `self._single_connection_client` (async mirror: `await self.initialize()`, which reads `self.single_connection_client`). `Pipeline` subclasses `Redis` but never runs `Redis.__init__`, so those attributes are unset and the README-documented flow

    with r.pipeline(transaction=False) as pipe:
        pipe.himport_prepare("users", [...])
        pipe.himport_set(...)

will raise `AttributeError` instead of registering the fieldset. No test exercises `pipe.himport_prepare` (the integration tests all call `himport_prepare` on the client and only `himport_set` on the pipe), so this path is uncovered. Either guard with `getattr(self, "_single_connection_client", False)` / override on `Pipeline`, or drop the pipeline form from the README. Note also that even when it works these methods execute immediately and return `bool`/`int` rather than the pipeline, so their results never appear in `execute()`'s result list — worth calling out in the docs.

The HIMPORT note added to `slave_for` is copy-pasted from `master_for` and ends with "(``himport_set`` is a write and is served by the master.)". A `slave_for` client connects to replicas, so `himport_set` issued through it will fail (READONLY), not be "served by the master". The same incorrect sentence was added to `redis/asyncio/sentinel.py::slave_for`. Either state that `himport_set` is unsupported on a replica client, or drop the write-related note from `slave_for`. (The async docstrings also read "Each call to current command returns a *new* client" — should be "method".)

`redis/commands/metadata.py` is written for Python 3.10+ but the project still advertises Python 3.9 support (README: "redis-py 6.2.0 supports Python 3.9+"), and this module has no `from __future__ import annotations`:

1. `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)` — the `slots` parameter was added in 3.10; on 3.9 this raises `TypeError: dataclass() got an unexpected keyword argument 'slots'` at import time. A future-import cannot fix this one.
2. PEP 604 unions in *evaluated* positions: the `CommandMetadata` field annotations (`request_policy: RequestPolicy | None = ...`), and the many method signatures such as `def resolve(self, command_name: str) -> CommandMetadata | None:` / `fallback: MetadataResolver | None = None`. Without `from __future__ import annotations` these are evaluated at class/def time and raise `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |` on 3.9.

Because `redis/cache.py` (and hence `redis/connection.py`/`redis/client.py`) now imports this module unconditionally, a failure here makes the whole package unimportable on 3.9, not just the new feature. Note the sibling modules touched by this PR (`redis/client.py`, `redis/asyncio/cluster.py`) deliberately use `from __future__ import annotations` for exactly this reason. The new async test module (`tests/test_asyncio/test_command_metadata.py`, `MetadataPolicyResolver.__init__`) has the same evaluated-union problem. Either add the future import and drop `slots=True`, or state the raised minimum Python version.

Deprecation versions for the same release are inconsistent: `STATIC_POLICIES` warns with `version="8.1.0"` (module `__getattr__`), while `CommandsParser.get_command_policies` / `AsyncCommandsParser.get_command_policies` are decorated with `@deprecated_function(version="8.2.0", ...)`. Both surfaces are deprecated by this PR, so the user-visible "deprecated since version X" strings should agree.

New module requires Python 3.10+ at import time. `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)` (`slots=` was added in 3.10) plus PEP 604 unions in *evaluated* positions — dataclass field annotations (`request_policy: RequestPolicy | None = ...`), method signatures (`def resolve(...) -> CommandMetadata | None`) and attribute-target annotations in `__init__` (`self._policies: dict[str, CommandPolicies | None] = {}`) — all execute at import. There is no `from __future__ import annotations` here, and `slots=True` would not be fixed by one anyway. Since `redis/cache.py` now imports this module, `import redis` fails outright on 3.9. Please confirm the declared `python_requires` (README still documents 3.9 support for 6.2.0+); if 3.9 is still supported, use `Optional[...]` and drop `slots=True` as the rest of the new code in `redis/_parsers/commands.py` does.

The documented recipe `StaticMetadataResolver(fallback=DynamicMetadataResolver(records))` passed as `metadata_resolver=` is safe for the standalone client but is a trap on `RedisCluster`: the same page states that routing is derived from `metadata_resolver` when no `policy_resolver` is given, so any command *absent* from the static table (e.g. DEL, UNLINK) resolves the server's `request_policy:multi_shard` tip — a policy that `_STATIC_COMMAND_METADATA` deliberately avoids recording because it is unimplemented in both stacks. The hazard and the `policy_resolver=StaticPolicyResolver()` workaround are documented only in the `RedisCluster` docstring; the docs page a user follows should carry the same warning next to the chained-resolver example.

`assert len(eligible - allow_list) == 53` pins an exact count derived from a live `COMMAND` reply, so any bump of the stack image (new module commands, or a module that starts reporting `readonly`/key specs) breaks CI for reasons unrelated to this client. Worse, the justifying comment says the number was measured on "Redis 8.9.241" while the test is gated on `STATIC_TABLE_SERVER_VERSION = "8.10.0"` — the count was measured on a server the gate now excludes, so it may already be wrong on the first server that runs it. Prefer asserting the invariants (nothing in the table is re-admitted; the named commands stay out) and drop the magic total, or gate the count on the exact image version it was measured against.

The comment justifying `_MEMO_MAX_ENTRIES` ("the default resolver a client gets is a single instance evaluated at import and shared by every client in the process") is contradicted by this same PR, which changed `policy_resolver`/`metadata_resolver` defaults to `None` so each client builds its own resolver (and the new tests assert exactly that). The same claim is repeated in the `BaseMetadataResolver`/`AsyncBaseMetadataResolver` docstrings. The cap is still worth keeping (unbounded command names memoize misses), but the stated rationale should be corrected so a future maintainer does not reason from it.
